findings.title: Findings converge on #60's "unused" verdict for project-rule pragmas
findings.why_it_matters: Three findings from both critics trace back to one thing #59 doesn't build: at #60, HSL900 will say a pragma naming a project rule is unused (parent D14). That verdict is why completeness has to be known at all (Finding 4). It is the main reason D1 retains bytes rather than paths (Finding 8). And the interim form of that verdict is why project-rule IDs sit in the per-file cache key (Finding 9). The question is whether this points at the verdict itself: should it be re-evaluated, including whether it's needed at all or whether stale project-rule pragmas are a limitation to accept, rather than resolving each finding on its own?
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate the project-rule "unused" verdict before addressing the converging findings. Open questions: does #60 keep the verdict; if not, what must a project rule's input retain; does a completeness concept still exist; do project-rule IDs still belong in the per-file cache key?
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate the project-rule "unused" verdict before addressing the converging findings. Open questions: does #60 keep the verdict; if not, what must a project rule's input retain; does a completeness concept still exist; do project-rule IDs still belong in the per-file cache key?
findings.choice_reason: Doesn't want current or future work shaped around something peers don't do; peers do validate suppressions, but not this cross-file verdict, so the verdict was dropped (D9).

findings.title: D7's TYPESCRIPT member and skip branch are production code with no shipped consumer
findings.why_it_matters: D7 (does #59 add a second language) adds `Language.TYPESCRIPT`, the `.ts` and `.tsx` suffixes, and a branch in `run_file_phase` that loads, retains, and counts a file without parsing, caching, or dispatching it. `PROJECT_RULES` ships empty, so nothing shipped can bring TypeScript into a scan. Only a test-registered rule reaches this path. D7's "Speculation: None" row also overstates: parent D7 ratified the suffixes, not the skip's semantics (counted in `files_scanned`, retained, no HSL900). The critics disagree: systems-architect considers the member and skip small, and says they make discovery testable on a real suffix.
findings.recommended: A: Keep D7 as ratified, correcting its Speculation row to say the skip's semantics are a placeholder #61 replaces.
findings.chosen: A: Keep D7 as ratified, correcting its Speculation row to say the skip's semantics are a placeholder #61 replaces.

findings.title: D5 and D7 contradict each other about whether HSL900 runs on every scanned file
findings.why_it_matters: D5 (which rules decide discovered languages) says HSL900 "runs on every file scanned" and "validates whatever is scanned". D7 says a TypeScript file in the scan is skipped, and "HSL900 doesn't reach it until #61". Both can't hold, and HSL900 is a plain `Rule` with no `languages`, so the real boundary lives in a hardcoded branch. "No analysis layer" is not stated anywhere as its own fact. If Finding 2 resolves to option C, D5's sentence becomes true as written and this finding is moot.
findings.recommended: A: Reword D5's recommendation and ratified sentence to say HSL900 validates every scanned file whose language has an analysis layer, with the skip branch as the one place that fact is decided.
findings.chosen: A: Reword D5's recommendation and ratified sentence to say HSL900 validates every scanned file whose language has an analysis layer, with the skip branch as the one place that fact is decided.

findings.title: "Output complete?" comes from more signals than D3 says, and D3 and D4 disagree
findings.why_it_matters: D3 (how a project rule reports failure) says #60's completeness flag is "whether the rule raised", and that completeness "can't disagree with whether there was an error". D4 (a file in the input fails to load) says #60 treats the output as incomplete after a load failure, when the rule did not raise. The Assumed section adds that explicit paths give a partial input until #39. A #60 builder following D3 literally would judge "unused suppression" on a partial input and report a false verdict. One oversized generated file is enough. Pylint's long-standing false `useless-suppression` warnings are this failure.
findings.recommended: A: Correct D3's deciding factor, table row, and ratified sentence to name both signals: the rule raised, or a file in that rule's input failed to load. #60 adds its flag and reads them directly.

findings.title: D2 adds a second candidate type and a location type before anything reads the grouping
findings.why_it_matters: D2 (what a project rule returns) adds `ProjectCandidate` and `Location` in a new `project_rule.py`, and expansion to `Finding`. `Finding` already holds a path and a validated position. At #59 "every finding from one candidate shares its message", so the grouping has no reader in this PR; its first reader is #60's `related` list and group id. systems-architect's pushback covers a different alternative (forcing locations into `CandidateFinding`, which is Python-flavoured), and doesn't answer returning `Finding`s.
findings.recommended: A: Keep D2, and have the build reuse `_validate_location` in `Location` rather than restating the checks.
findings.chosen: A: Keep D2, and have the build reuse `_validate_location` in `Location` rather than restating the checks.

findings.title: D3 and D4 define several failure paths for a rule kind with no rules
findings.why_it_matters: The project phase has three separate behaviours: `ProjectRuleFailure` becomes an error and later rules still run; an unexpected exception becomes `internal_error` and later rules stop; and a file-phase abort skips the phase. The critic's simplification is one catch that turns any exception into one `LintError` carrying `str(exc)`, exit 3, then continue. Its claim that there is "no bug/expected split to defend" runs into the existing CLI, where exit 4 means internal and exit 3 means operational. Under that catch, a wrapper bug would surface as exit 3 with a message such as `'firstFile'`, and `internal_error` deliberately hides that detail.
findings.recommended: A: Keep D3 and D4 as ratified.
findings.chosen: A: Keep D3 and D4 as ratified.

findings.title: Discovery's language set and the applies check answer one question in two places
findings.why_it_matters: D6 (does discovery call the applies check) deliberately splits the decision: discovery unions `languages` over enabled ordinary rules, and everything after discovery calls the check. The split is what keeps a file that every rule ignores in the scan, and structural-minimalist also says to keep it. The cost is that a later applicability input, such as the config extension map `language.py` anticipates, needs a change in both places, and a mismatch is silent: a file gets discovered, loaded, and counted with no rule handling it. The ledger gives the check a home in `config.py` but says only "computed from the config" for the union.
findings.recommended: A: Keep D6's split, and add to New homes that the function computing discovery's languages lives in `config.py` beside the applies check.
findings.chosen: A: Keep D6's split, and add to New homes that the function computing discovery's languages lives in `config.py` beside the applies check.

findings.title: D1 retains bytes for a consumer that #59 defers to #60
findings.why_it_matters: D1 (what a project rule receives) retains `LoadedFile`s, but jscpd needs only paths and the bytes consumer is #60's pragma re-parse, which is out of scope here. If #60 dropped its unused-pragma verdict, the bytes might never be needed, and D1's own "Pick B instead if" says so. The critic also concedes that the rest of the engine is identical either way, so there's no shape cost: the retained list exists under both options, and only its element type differs.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: `LoadedFile`s are retained with no reader of their bytes until #60 lands.

findings.title: Project-rule IDs stay in the per-file cache key for a verdict that moves out at #60
findings.why_it_matters: Project-rule IDs have to stay in the key at #59, because the interim pragma verdict reads `enabled_rules`. Parent D14 then moves the unused and disabled verdicts to the project phase, after which the key no longer needs those IDs. If #60 doesn't narrow it, toggling a project rule invalidates every Python file's cache entry for no reason, costing one cold run of about 7 seconds on hassette.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: toggling a project rule invalidates the per-file cache until #60 narrows the key.
